summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a migration/parity demo for NimblePay who currently use OpenAI and Together models. Core focus: API parity, streaming and function-calling differences, cost/latency tradeoffs, deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs VPC), and security/compliance. Agreed next steps: send parity mapping, provision trial key, run benchmarks with NimblePay prompts, and follow up on security docs and pricing.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. We'll do a quick 35-45 minute demo showing how to map your OpenAI/Anthropic/Together usage over to Redwood API and where parity is good or needs small changes. Priya the SE will drive the demo.
[00:12] Jenna Ortiz: Hi Alex, thanks. We have about 40 minutes, trying to make sure we cover streaming, function-calling parity and also security stuff—Sana will ask the security Qs.
[00:20] Priya Rao: Great. Quick intros, Marco from Product is on too, hey Marco.
[00:25] Marco Li: hi all.
[00:30] Marcus Bell: Marcus, platform. We mostly run inference via OpenAI for chat completions and Together for some low-latency use cases.
[00:36] Alex Chen: Perfect, can you briefly describe your traffic pattern and what you're optimizing for?
[00:42] Marcus Bell: Yeah, typical traffic is 5k reqs/min at peak across two endpoints. Avg prompt length around 350 tokens, replies average 120 tokens. We do a mix of synchronous chat and streaming for our assistant product. Cost is a big driver, and we have strict latency SLOs under 300ms tail for streaming starts.
[01:05] Priya Rao: Awesome. So objective for demo: show the Redwood API mapping for completions and chat, streaming behaviour, function-like structured outputs (we have structured output tooling), and the Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization to reduce unit cost.
[01:18] Jenna Ortiz: Quick question before you jump in: do we need to rewrite prompts? We have a lot of prompt engineering invested in OpenAI format.
[01:25] Priya Rao: Short answer: mostly no. Redwood supports an OpenAI-compatible REST surface for text generation and chat. Where you might change is model-name substitutions and a few params. For Anthropic we map to Redwood models with slightly different temperature semantics, and for Together the main difference is how the chunked streaming arrives but payloads are compatible. We'll show concrete examples.
[01:45] Sana Iqbal: And from security, can you confirm data residency and KMS options for private deployments? We need audit logs for every request.
[01:52] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll cover that. Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC and integrates with KMS/HSM for envelope encryption. Audit logs are available and we have SOC2 and ISO artifacts to share. We'll attach the security pack after the call.
[02:08] Priya Rao: Okay jumping into the console share. I'm going to demo a mapping doc, then run a live call. Note: the console UI shown is demo and the team will give you a repo with equivalent curl/SDK examples.
[02:20] [screen share noise / switching windows]
[02:35] Priya Rao: Here is an excerpt of a parity spreadsheet. Column A is your current provider/model (e.g., gpt-4o, claude-2, together-mini), Column B is Redwood model equivalent, Column C has parameter notes (temperature mapping, top_p, tokens / max_length recommendation). For example, OpenAI gpt-4o -> redwood-large-v2 with recommended context length 8k and set context_window param.
[02:58] Priya Rao: For Anthropic style prompts where you use system + user turns, Redwood chat API supports the same role type and you can map system to system role; but note that the sampling temperature range is 0-1 but some Anthropic variants report slightly different default smoothing, so we recommend running a short eval.
[03:20] Jenna Ortiz: When you say "map" models, is there a definitive 1:1? We have certain safety and style requirements and we tuned to Claude outputs.
[03:27] Priya Rao: There's no perfect 1:1 for every case — quality differs slightly. We provide a model catalog with performance profiles and example outputs. For your sensitive flows we'll run a parity evaluation during POC and iterate on prompt tweaks and small fine-tuning / instruction templates if needed.
[03:45] [crosstalk] Tyler Wu: Are you able to run our prompt set against both our current models and Redwood to show diffs?
[03:50] Alex Chen: Yep, that's part of the benchmark run we proposed. Priya will take your prompt set and run side-by-side comparisons and send a report.
[04:00] Priya Rao: Now I'll do a live API demo. First, a simple chat completion using an OpenAI-style request. Note — we'll call the Redwood hosted endpoint with an API key.
[04:15] [typing sounds]
[04:22] Priya Rao: Ok sending request... The response streams back, you'll see chunked events similar to OpenAI Server Sent Events. [shows streaming tokens appearing slightly faster] See, the streaming start latency is about 180ms in this region on our hosted cluster.
[04:40] Marcus Bell: That looks good. How about token accounting? We bill per-response tokens?
[04:45] Alex Chen: For hosted, billing is per-token for input + output. For Dedicated we can do committed capacity pricing with predictable unit cost. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching/kv cache to reduce token re-generation.
[05:00] Jenna Ortiz: Marcus — do you use function calling heavily?
[05:04] Marcus Bell: Yes for some of the orchestration paths. We call external tools via structured JSON responses.
[05:09] Priya Rao: Redwood supports function / tool calling patterns. We have a structured output mode where you can declare a JSON schema or a function set and the model returns JSON payloads. The mapping from OpenAI's function_call param is essentially identical; small syntactic rename in some SDKs but same semantics. I'll demo a function call now.
[05:27] [screen demo]
[05:31] Priya Rao: Here's a function contract (get_account_balance). I'm sending a chat with function_call: 'auto'. You'll see the model returns a structured JSON and we pipe that to your service.
[05:40] Jenna Ortiz: Great. Any differences in failure modes? Like partial JSON or malformed returns?
[05:45] Priya Rao: Same class of issues as any LLM provider. We add a structured-output validator in the SDK that can auto-retry with different temperature or request the model to reformat. That's part of Redwood's higher-level SDK utilities.
[05:59] Tyler Wu: On latency, you mentioned 180ms for stream start. Our tail p95 matters. What's typical p95 with your hosted clusters?
[06:06] Alex Chen: For the models similar to gpt-4o equivalency running on our hosted fleet, p95 stream start is usually 200-350ms depending on prompt length and KV cache hit rates. For Dedicated on pinned GPUs we can hit lower and more consistent p95s — often under 200ms.
[06:22] Marcus Bell: Important for us — Together had a smaller cost but lower quality in some cases; can Redwood run quantized models to get Together-like cost with better quality?
[06:31] Priya Rao: Yes — Optimize recommends quantization profiles. We support int8/4 quantization options and model compilation that preserves most quality while cutting GPU memory and cost. The tradeoff is a small accuracy delta which we quantify in the evals.
[06:47] Alex Chen: Also caching — our KV/prefix cache prevents repeated token generation on common prefixes which reduces tail latency and cost. For assistant-style flows with repeated prompts that helps a lot.
[06:58] Jenna Ortiz: Ok good. Moving to security: Sana, anything specific now?
[07:04] Sana Iqbal: Yes. KMS integration for key rotation, audit log retention policy, whether logs can be forwarded to our SIEM, and how PII is handled in transit at rest. Also, do you support customer-managed encryption keys in cloud provider KMS?
[07:16] Alex Chen: Short answers: yes to KMS integration and customer-managed keys in Private deployments; audit logs can be shipped to S3/Cloud Storage or forwarded to syslog/our ingestion. We'll share specifics in the security pack. For hosted API, we keep request logs for X days by default but can extend or limit retention under enterprise agreements.
[07:38] Priya Rao: Also for Private, you can disable request-level retention and only keep aggregated metrics.
[07:44] Sana Iqbal: Good. Do you have SOC2 report and pen test summary?
[07:48] Alex Chen: Yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO artifacts are in the security pack; we'll send them after this meeting.
[07:55] [brief pause]
[08:02] Priya Rao: Back to the demo — I'm going to show a tiny SDK snippet for migrating from OpenAI. Example: replace openai.ChatCompletion.create with redwood.chat.create, same messages array, change model parameter to a Redwood model name, and keep temperature/top_p. Error handling and streaming hooks are similar.
[08:24] Priya Rao: Note: anthology style responses sometimes need small prompt-format change for personality/shaping. We'll help with recommended templates.
[08:33] Marcus Bell: Any breaking API changes versus Together? We use Together's streaming websocket for lower latency.
[08:39] Priya Rao: Redwood supports websocket streaming and SSE depending on your preference. Together users often migrate to Redwood websocket streaming with minimal changes. For payload formats we can provide an adapter library that mimics Together's client semantics.
[08:54] Jenna Ortiz: Can we do a quick run showing our prompt set? We sent a short sample earlier this week.
[08:59] Alex Chen: Yes, Priya has your sample file. Priya, can you run a couple of prompts with both OpenAI and Redwood for a quick diff?
[09:06] Priya Rao: Running now — I'll run side-by-side locally, will paste the outputs. [typing] Ok first prompt: "invoice assistant summarise latest statement". OpenAI reply excerpt: "summary..." Redwood reply: "summary... slight stylistic difference, more concise." You can see tone differences; we can tune via system message.
[09:35] Jenna Ortiz: Those look close enough; we can live with a small tone tweak.
[09:39] Priya Rao: Next, a function-call prompt. OpenAI returned JSON with account id, Redwood returned same structure but added an extra confidence field we can drop. That can be normalized in our SDK.
[09:54] Tyler Wu: For benchmarking, we'll want to measure cost per 1M tokens estimate, and latency under our 95th tail with our payloads.
[10:02] Alex Chen: Understood. We'll include tokenized cost projection in the pricing sheet and run the POC benchmark in your AWS region to match latency.
[10:12] Marcus Bell: On Dedicated — quick clarification — if we pin GPUs, do you also support autoscaling burst to hosted capacity?
[10:19] Alex Chen: Yes, we have burst policies where Dedicated can overflow to Redwood hosted pools for transient peaks, with configurable fallback rules and quotas. That helps avoid overprovisioning.
[10:30] Marcus Bell: Nice. Jenna: any procurement timeline constraints?
[10:33] Jenna Ortiz: We're aiming to select a vendor end of quarter, so we need a quick POC and security sign-offs by mid-April.
[10:42] Alex Chen: OK we'll aim for that. Priya will run benchmark and Priya + Marco will own quality tuning.
[10:50] Priya Rao: Two quick advanced notes: 1) For KV cache warmed by user sessions, we support session affinity in routing so the same KV stays hot. 2) For reranking/embeddings replacement from your Together pipelines, Redwood embedding models map one-to-one, but reranking might need slight embedding model selection. We'll include recommendations.
[11:13] Jenna Ortiz: One more security Q — can we do an on-prem install or air-gapped for regulated flows?
[11:18] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Private has an on-prem package that can be run air-gapped. There are some operational requirements (disk encryption, local KMS/ HSM). We'll include the deployment checklist.
[11:30] [brief interruption]
[11:36] Priya Rao: Final part of demo is Redwood Optimize. This is a recommendations UI that looks at trace-level token distributions and suggests batch sizes, quantization, and model substitution for cold vs hot paths. For example, we recommended switching a low-variance helper flow from redwood-large to redwood-medium-quant with int8 which reduced cost by ~40% with minimal quality loss in similar customers.
[11:58] Marcus Bell: That is compelling. Do you require us to send traces or do you have an in-console profiler?
[12:05] Priya Rao: We ingest anonymized traces (you control PII redaction) or you can run the profiler agent in your environment for Dedicated. The Optimize recommendations are delivered as a config suggestion and you can apply them or rollout via canary.
[12:20] Jenna Ortiz: Great. Time check — about 10 minutes left. Any final questions?
[12:25] Sana Iqbal: One more: incident response SLAs and runbook access?
[12:29] Alex Chen: Enterprise support tiers include runbook access, 24/7 paging for Severity 1 incidents and a dedicated CSM for onboarding. We'll include the SLA summary and support contacts.
[12:42] Marcus Bell: For the POC, we want scoped success criteria: parity on main invoice summarization flow (quality within 5% of current), streaming start p95 under 300ms, and cost <= current baseline or a clear path to cost parity with quantization.
[12:58] Alex Chen: Agreed — we'll formalize that in the POC doc.
[13:05] Jenna Ortiz: Ok let's recap next steps.
[13:08] Alex Chen: Action items: we'll send parity mapping spreadsheet, security pack (SOC2/ISO and KMS info), trial API key + sample repo, benchmark plan and pricing sheet. Priya will run the benchmark and send results. Marcus, you'll share traffic profile and prompt set. Sana will confirm security checklist items you need.
[13:26] Jenna Ortiz: Sounds good. Thanks Alex/Priya/Marco. We'll review materials and schedule the benchmark kickoff.
[13:33] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by EOD with docs.
[13:38] [call ends]
